title: C++ Lambdas Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on C++ lambdas: syntax, capture semantics, mutable and generic lambdas, std::function vs templates, function objects, and dangling-capture pitfalls.

chapters.title: Lambda Anatomy and Mental Model
points: A lambda is syntactic sugar for an unnamed closure class with an operator() (const by default); the lambda expression creates one closure object
Syntax: [captures](params) specifiers -> ret { body }; the return type is deduced and -> ret is only needed when return statements disagree
Each lambda expression has a unique closure type, so two identical-looking lambdas have different types
Captureless lambdas convert implicitly to a plain function pointer; capturing ones do not
Example: auto add = [](int a, int b){ return a + b; }; add(2,3) // 5

chapters.title: Captures: Value, Reference, Mutable
points: [x] copies x at closure creation time, so later changes to the original are not seen; [&x] refers to the original
[=] captures all used locals by value and [&] by reference; mix them as [=, &y] or [&, x]
The by-value copy is const inside operator(); add mutable to modify the copy: [n]() mutable { return ++n; } (the original is unchanged)
Init-capture (C++14): [p = std::move(ptr)] or [v = x*2] allows move-only capture and computed members
[this] captures the pointer, not the object; [*this] (C++17) copies the whole object; [=] no longer implicitly captures this in C++20

chapters.title: Generic Lambdas and Function Objects
points: auto parameters (C++14) make operator() a template: [](auto a, auto b){ return a + b; } works with int, double, std::string
C++20 template lambda: []<typename T>(std::vector<T>& v){ ... } gives access to T and constrains the argument shape
Hand-written function object: struct Add { int operator()(int a, int b) const { return a+b; } }; it can hold state and be reused as a named type
std::plus<>, std::greater<>, std::less<> are standard function objects; the transparent <> form deduces the types
Lambda vs functor: the lambda is shorter and local; use a named functor when you need the type in several places or have multiple overloads

chapters.title: std::function vs Templates
points: Template parameter (template<class F> void run(F f)) keeps the exact closure type, so the call is inlinable with no allocation: the fastest option

std::function<R(Args...)> type-erases any callable: it can be stored in members and containers and have different callables assigned, but costs an indirect call and possibly a heap allocation for large captures
std::function requires a copyable callable, so a move-only lambda fails; use std::move_only_function (C++23) or a template instead
Rule of thumb: templates for parameters that are called immediately; std::function for stored or runtime-swapped callbacks; function_ref or a function pointer for cheap non-owning params
Example: std::vector<std::function<void()>> tasks; tasks.push_back([&]{ work(); }); mixes different lambdas in one container

chapters.title: Dangling Captures and Common Mistakes
points: Returning or storing a lambda with [&] after the locals die leaves dangling references (undefined behavior): auto f(){ int x=1; return [&]{ return x; }; }
Fix: capture by value or init-capture (return [x]{ return x; };), and never let a reference-capturing lambda outlive its scope (threads, async, stored callbacks)
[this] in a callback outliving the object is a dangling pointer; use [*this], or capture shared_from_this() via [self = shared_from_this()]
A mutable by-value lambda copied into std::function or an algorithm works on the copy, so state is lost; use [&] or std::ref if you need shared state
Default capture [=]/[&] hides what is captured: prefer explicit captures in anything stored or asynchronous

chapters.title: Lambda Cheat Sheet
points: Syntax: [capture](params) mutable constexpr noexcept -> ret { body }; the capture list is the only mandatory part besides {}
Capture table: [x] copy | [&x] ref | [=] all by copy | [&] all by ref | [x=expr] init | [this] pointer | [*this] copy of the object
Choose a callable type: template F for calls inside the function | std::function for stored or swappable | function pointer for captureless C APIs
Safe rules: by value for anything escaping scope; by reference only for immediate use (std::sort, for_each); move-only via init-capture

Interview Point: why is a lambda's operator() const by default, and what does mutable change? | when would you prefer a template parameter over std::function? | what undefined behavior can [&] cause in a returned lambda? | how do you capture a unique_ptr?
